title: Question 8
stem:
The circuit of an inverting amplifier incorporating an ideal operational amplifier (op-amp) is shown in Fig. 8.1.

{{figure:figure_8_1}}

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Explain why point $P$ is known as a virtual earth.

markscheme_points.text: V+ is at earth potential so P (or V-) must be at earth

hints: Hint 1: Start by looking at the + input in Fig. 8.1. Where is it connected, and what voltage must it therefore be at?
Hint 2: Remember the key property of an ideal op-amp - its open-loop gain is extremely large. What would happen to the output if the two inputs differed by even a tiny voltage?
Hint 3: For the amplifier to work normally without saturating, what must be true about the voltage difference between the - input (point P) and the + input?
parts.proper_answer: Ideal op-amp has very large open-loop gain, so it saturates unless $V_{+} \approx V_{-}$. Since $V_{+}$ is connected to earth ($0\text{ V}$), $V_{-}$ at point P must also be at $≈0\text{ V}$ without being directly connected to earth. Hence P is a virtual earth.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot the earth on the non-inverting input**
You are sitting with the circuit, so first trace the + input. It goes straight down to the earth rail. That means $V_{+} = 0\text{ V}$ always. Point P is the - input, so the question is really: why must P copy that 0 V?

Step 2: **Use the huge gain of the ideal op-amp**
An ideal op-amp multiplies the difference between its inputs by an enormous number: $$V_{OUT} = A_{0}(V_{+} - V_{-})$$ where $A_{0}$ is infinite or very large. Even a difference of a millivolt would try to drive $V_{OUT}$ beyond the $\pm V$ supplies. In practice the op-amp would saturate.

Step 3: **Force P to follow the earth**
To stay in linear operation and not saturate, we must have $V_{+} - V_{-} \approx 0$. So $V_{-} \approx V_{+}$. Since $V_{+} = 0$, point P is held at about $0\text{ V}$. It behaves like earth for voltage, but no earth wire is there and current does not flow to earth from P, so we call it a virtual earth.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
Derive an expression, in terms of the resistances $R_1$ and $R_2$, for the gain of the amplifier circuit.
Explain your working.

markscheme_points.text: input resistance to op-amp is very large or current in R2 = current in R1

hints: Hint 1: An ideal op-amp draws no current at its inputs because its input resistance is very large. If no current enters P from the op-amp, where must the current through $R_{2}$ go?
Hint 2: Use the virtual earth idea from (a). If P is at $0\text{ V}$, what is the p.d. across $R_{2}$ in terms of $V_{IN}$, and the p.d. across $R_{1}$ in terms of $V_{OUT}$?
Hint 3: Write Ohm's law $I = V/R$ for each resistor using the same current $I$, then divide the two equations to eliminate $I$ and find $V_{OUT}/V_{IN}$.
parts.proper_answer: No current enters ideal op-amp, so current $I$ in $R_{2}$ equals current in $R_{1}$. With P at $0\text{ V}$: $V_{IN} - 0 = IR_{2}$ and $0 - V_{OUT} = IR_{1}$. Dividing gives $V_{OUT}/V_{IN} = -R_{1}/R_{2}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Realise one current flows through both resistors**
Think of point P as a junction. Current arrives through $R_{2}$, but it cannot go into the - input because an ideal op-amp has infinite input resistance. So all of it must leave through the feedback resistor $R_{1}$. Call this common current $I$.

Step 2: **Apply Ohm's law to each resistor using virtual earth**
From (a), $V_{P} = 0$. For $R_{2}$, the left end is at $V_{IN}$ and the right end is at 0, so: $$V_{IN} - 0 = IR_{2}$$ For $R_{1}$, the left end is at 0 and the right end is at $V_{OUT}$, so: $$0 - V_{OUT} = IR_{1}$$ Notice the minus sign appears because $V_{OUT}$ will be opposite in sign to $V_{IN}$.

Step 3: **Combine to get the closed-loop gain**
Both expressions equal the same $I$, so divide them: $$\frac{-V_{OUT}}{V_{IN}} = \frac{IR_{1}}{IR_{2}}$$ Cancelling $I$ gives: $$\frac{V_{OUT}}{V_{IN}} = -\frac{R_{1}}{R_{2}}$$ The negative sign tells you it is inverting - a positive input gives a negative output.

parts.label: (c)

markscheme_points.text: relay coil connected between VOUT and earth
correct diode symbol connected between VOUT and coil or between coil and earth

hints: Hint 1: A relay coil needs a current through it to earth to close the switch. Between which two points in Fig. 8.2 must the coil be connected to get current from $V_{OUT}$?
Hint 2: A diode conducts in one direction only. To allow operation for positive $V_{OUT}$ but block it for negative $V_{OUT}$, should the diode be in series with the coil or in a separate branch?
Hint 3: Check polarity. For conventional current to flow from a positive $V_{OUT}$ down through the coil to earth, which way must the diode arrow point?
parts.proper_answer: Connect the relay coil in series with a diode between the $V_{OUT}$ terminal and earth. Diode anode towards $V_{OUT}$ (cathode towards coil/earth) so forward conduction is from $V_{OUT}$ to earth. Current flows and relay operates only when $V_{OUT}$ is positive.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Provide a path for output current through the relay**
The relay is just an electromagnet coil. One end must go to the $V_{OUT}$ top wire and the other end must go to the earth bottom wire. Then a voltage $V_{OUT}$ will try to push current through the coil to earth.

Step 2: **Add a diode in series to select polarity**
A diode is a one-way valve. Put it in series with the coil, either between $V_{OUT}$ and the coil or between the coil and earth. When forward biased it conducts with almost zero resistance, when reverse biased it blocks.

Step 3: **Orient the diode for positive-only operation**
You want conduction when $V_{OUT}$ is positive. Conventional current must flow downwards from $V_{OUT}$ to earth. So the diode symbol must point downwards, anode up to $V_{OUT}$ and cathode down toward earth. For negative $V_{OUT}$ the diode is reverse biased, no current flows, and the relay stays off.
